Godhuli Dairy Cloud: Annexure C

A four-year tender, a slide that became a contract, and three documents that all answer to the same name

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Deepa Ranganathan was still at her desk on the fourth floor of Godhuli Dairy Cloud's office in Baner, Pune, with the ceiling fans switched off and the monsoon finally gone out of the air. Three files were open on her laptop. The first was a 62-slide deck titled Godhuli 2029, written eighteen months earlier for a Series B raise and since then sent, in whole or in part, to investors, customers, two state governments and at least one journalist. The second was a tender response due at 5 p.m. on Friday, 9 October, to the Dhaval Milk Producers Union — ₹19 crore over four years, the largest single contract Godhuli had ever bid for, with a procurement template that awarded twenty of its hundred marks to a dated schedule of feature delivery to be attached as Annexure C and incorporated into the contract by reference. The third was a spreadsheet her VP Engineering had sent at 9:40 that evening with the subject line "commitment register — please read before you send anything."

The three files disagreed with one another. Slide 14 of Godhuli 2029 listed eleven capabilities against calendar quarters. The commitment register listed nine items, four of them with different names, and only two with dates that engineering had agreed to. Somewhere between those two documents sat the Q2 OKR scorecard the board would see on the morning of Friday, 9 October — four hours before the tender was due — reporting an attainment of 0.72 against a quarter in which, by Deepa's own count, less than half of what had been promised had shipped. She had been asked, that afternoon, by two different people, to “just send the plan.”

2. Company history

Godhuli Dairy Cloud was founded in Pune in 2017 by Vikram Sethi, who had spent nine years running chilling-centre operations for a private milk processor in western Maharashtra, and Renuka Pathak, an embedded-systems engineer from Nashik. By 2026 it sold five modules to co-operative unions, producer companies and private dairies across nine states, on annual recurring revenue of ₹61 crore.

The decision that constrained everything Deepa could do in October 2026 had been taken in March 2021, before she joined (Exhibit 4). Bidding for its first state federation contract, Godhuli had been asked by the buyer's procurement officer for “the product plan.” Vikram had sent the roadmap slide from the Series A deck. The officer attached it to the contract as Annexure C, with a liquidated-damages clause of 0.5 per cent of contract value for every week a listed item was late, capped at 7.5 per cent. Godhuli won the tender. It also, without quite noticing, published a template. Procurement officers in the dairy co-operative sector talk to one another, and the annexure — a dated grid of named features, signed by the vendor — began appearing in tender documents that Godhuli had never seen before. By 2026 three of the company's four largest customers had a version of it in their contracts, and the Dhaval tender's scoring sheet asked for twenty-four months of it.

3. The industry

India produces more milk than any other country, and roughly half of what is formally collected moves through co-operative structures descended from the Anand pattern — Amul's federation, Mother Dairy, and the state unions that the National Dairy Development Board has spent decades organising. Alongside them sit listed private processors such as Hatsun, Heritage Foods and Dodla, who buy milk from the same villages on price and reliability.

Three forces bore directly on Godhuli's product. The first was payments. Farmer payouts had moved almost entirely to bank transfer and UPI rails operated under NPCI, which made ten-day payment cycles look archaic and put pressure on Godhuli to reconcile within twenty-four hours. The second was data law. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act had turned the farmer's fat-and-SNF history, Aadhaar-linked payout record and herd data into personal data requiring consent and purpose limitation — a problem when the consent-giver is a farmer with a feature phone and the data controller is a union with nine clerks. The third was quality enforcement: FSSAI's tightening of adulteration norms had made anomaly detection at the collection point commercially interesting, which was why Godhuli had hired a data scientist in Toronto.

Godhuli's exposure was no longer only Indian. In July 2026 it had signed a ₹2.4 crore pilot with Darpan Foods Trading LLC, a Dubai importer distributing UHT milk, paneer and ghee across the UAE and Oman, which wanted lot-level traceability from Indian village to Gulf shelf. A second front had opened in East Africa, where two Kenyan dairy co-operatives were running Godhuli's collection module on 2G. Both markets bought the same slide 14.

4. The situation in detail

The sequence mattered more than any single event. In October 2024, three months after the Series B closed, Vikram introduced OKRs across the company after a board conversation about “focus.” Product teams, asked for key results in a fortnight, did the natural thing: they copied the rows of the capability calendar and put “ship” in front of each one. From that quarter onwards, a slide written to persuade investors of a five-year direction was also the company's quarterly scorecard.

In August 2025, Godhuli had won its first Dhaval contract — ₹7.8 crore over three years for 2,300 collection centres — on a bid that scored well precisely because slide 14 was dated and the competing bid was not.

Then two assumptions failed. The first was capacity. The capacity model behind slide 14 assumed forty engineers by April 2026; attrition in Bengaluru and a hiring freeze imposed in March, when the board asked for eighteen months of runway, left thirty-one (Exhibit 5), of whom four were on the Darpan integration. The second was hardware. The chilling-centre telemetry module depended on in-line analysers from Ganak Sensor Instruments, whose FSSAI certification for the new model took fourteen weeks longer than the supplier had indicated. Telemetry went live in January 2026 instead of October 2025. Under Annexure C, Dhaval accrued ₹35 lakh in liquidated damages. Dhaval's managing director waived them — in exchange for the quality-anomaly module being added to the existing contract at no charge, a concession recorded in an email and never scoped by engineering. That unscoped concession now sat inside the commitment register as an open item with no date (Exhibit 3, row 6), and it was one of the eleven things slide 14 promised Dhaval's parent federation in the new tender.

What had since turned out to be wrong ran deeper than two slipped dates. Nobody in the company could say, when Deepa had asked in September, which document was the one that governed: the deck, the calendar, the register or the OKR sheet.

5. The people

Deepa Ranganathan — Chief Product Officer, Pune. Joined in August 2025 from a Bengaluru logistics software company. Position: nothing dated should leave the building unless engineering has resourced it. Incentive: her equity vests against a Series C that needs both the tender win and a credible growth story. Not saying: she approved the February edit of slide 14 herself, without checking the capacity model behind it.
Vikram Sethi — Co-founder and CEO, Pune. Position: the 2029 deck is the company's argument and must not be diluted into a list of quarters; Godhuli sells a direction, not a feature list. Incentive: Series C conversations are open with two funds, and a shortened horizon reads as retreat. Not saying: he has already shown slide 14 to one of those funds as evidence of execution discipline.
Harpreet Bedi — VP Engineering, Bengaluru. Position: no customer-facing document should carry a date beyond the current quarter; the register is the only truth. Incentive: his team's variable pay is tied to “plan attainment,” which rewards a short, conservative plan. Not saying: two of the four items he has marked amber in the register are amber because he moved engineers onto the Darpan integration without telling anyone.
Farida Contractor — Director, International Business, Dubai. Position: the Gulf buyer will not sign a renewal without dates, and Darpan's ₹2.4 crore pilot converts to ₹6 crore annually if traceability goes live on 1 January 2027. Incentive: commission on booked value at signature, not at go-live. Not saying: she has already sent Darpan's procurement head a version of slide 14 with two rows pulled forward by a quarter, to match the go-live date in the pilot contract.
Sandeep Mule — Director, Field Implementation, Nashik. Position: the rollout schedule in the tender is arithmetically impossible with the installation crews available, whatever the software does. Incentive: he is measured on centres activated per month and will be blamed for a slow ramp he did not design. Not saying: he has been quietly slowing activations at two unions to keep his support queue manageable, which is part of why field-readiness looks better than it is.
Dr Ayesha Qureshi — Principal Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: the quality-anomaly model must not be named in a contract until it has run a full flush season; false positives accuse farmers of adulteration, and a wrong accusation at a collection centre is not a software bug. Incentive: her OKR is model precision, which improves by shipping later. Not saying: she believes the model is already good enough for the co-operative use case and is holding for the harder export use case that Farida sold.
Ritu Kapadia — Partner, Gopuram Growth Partners, Mumbai; board member. Position: wants the board pack to show outcome metrics — centres live, payout latency, net revenue retention — rather than feature lists. Incentive: she is marking Godhuli for her fund's own year-end review and needs the 2029 thesis intact. Not saying: it was her “focus” comment in 2024 that produced the OKR system now generating the numbers she distrusts.

7. Voices

“Please do not send the calendar. I will give you a schedule for what we can actually do in this quarter and the next, and after that I will give you themes. If you put Q4 FY28 in a tender I will not sign it, and if I do not sign it you should not either.” Harpreet Bedi to Deepa Ranganathan, internal chat, 6 October 2026, 9:44 p.m.
“The buyer's template gives twenty marks for the delivery schedule. Twenty. We lost a bid in Gujarat last year on eleven. I understand everything engineering is saying. I am asking a different question: do we want to bid or not?” Farida Contractor, tender review call, 5 October 2026, 7:00 a.m. Gulf time.
“A false positive is a man being told at 5 in the morning, in front of his neighbours, that he has watered his milk. I will not have that sentence in a contract with a date on it.” Dr Ayesha Qureshi, product review, 29 September 2026.
“The 2029 story is what got us ₹210 crore and it is what will get us the next round. Every time we cut it down to eight quarters we sound like a services company. Deepa, send the board the story and send the union the schedule. They are different audiences.” Vikram Sethi, email to Deepa Ranganathan, 6 October 2026.
“May I ask a simple question. When the attainment number moved from 0.51 to 0.72, who approved that, and did the customer commitments move by the same amount?” Ritu Kapadia, board pre-read comment, 5 October 2026.

8. The options as Deepa sees them

Option A — Bid as the template asks

Generate Annexure C from slide 14, extend it to twenty-four months, submit by Friday. It also signs Godhuli to eleven dated capabilities of which engineering has agreed to two, against a damages cap of ₹1.43 crore (Exhibit 6), on a rollout schedule that Sandeep says is ten months short before a line of code is written.

Option B — Bid with an outcome annexure

Replace the feature grid with committed outcomes: payout latency under twenty-four hours, centre uptime, activation rate per crew, a quality-service availability target. Argue to the union that outcomes are what they are actually buying. The risk is arithmetic: the scoring sheet allots twenty marks to a dated feature schedule, and nobody at Godhuli knows whether an outcome annexure scores twenty, ten or zero. The union's tender committee has never seen one.

Option C — Separate the documents

Keep Godhuli 2029 as an investor narrative, publish an eighteen-month themed view with no dates for customers, and let only the commitment register carry dates into contracts. This is closest to what Harpreet and Nandita want. It requires telling Vikram that slide 14 must stop circulating four days before he presents to the board, and telling Farida that Darpan's renewal conversation loses the page she has been selling from.

Nandita Bose, the head of design in London, had written her one line of comment on this list on Monday and Deepa had not answered it: “All three of these are about what we write down. None of them is about the fact that we pay Farida at signature, pay Harpreet for attainment and pay Sandeep for activations, and then ask the three of them to agree on one page.”

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The tender closed at 5 p.m. on Friday, 9 October 2026, with an earnest-money deposit of ₹38 lakh already lodged and forfeit only on withdrawal after award. The hiring freeze ran to the end of Q4 FY27; thirty-one engineers was the number Deepa had, at ₹34 lakh fully loaded each, and four of them were committed to Darpan's 1 January 2027 go-live, which carried a ten per cent holdback on the ₹2.4 crore if it slipped. The Dhaval managing director's waiver email — the one that had cost ₹35 lakh in forgiven damages and bought an unscoped module — was, Deepa's legal counsel had told her that afternoon, probably enforceable.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Take each of the five artefacts in Exhibit 1. What promise does each one make, to whom, and for how long? Where do those promises contradict one another?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 describe the same product. Read them together: what exactly has Godhuli told the market that it cannot support, and how much of that gap is a communication problem rather than a delivery problem?
  3. Exhibit 5 reports attainment of 0.72 and delivery of 41 per cent. Both numbers are defensible. What would you need to know to decide which one the board should be shown, and what does the existence of both tell you about the system that produced them?
  4. The 2021 annexure decision was made in an afternoon and has shaped five years of contracting. Which decision being taken this week is the equivalent, and how would you recognise it at the time?
  5. Nandita argues that the incentive structure, not the documentation, is the problem. If she is right, do any of Deepa's three options help? What would a fifth option look like, and who would have to lose something for it to work?
  6. It is Monday, 12 October, and the tender has been submitted in whichever form you chose. What are Deepa's first three actions that morning, in order, and what does she say to the board about the difference between what Godhuli intends, what it has scheduled and what it has signed?

11. Later that night

Farida's message arrived at 12:22 a.m. Gulf time, a single line asking whether she could tell Darpan that traceability was confirmed for January. Harpreet's register was still open on the second screen, row 5 in red. On Friday morning Vikram would stand in front of Ritu Kapadia and describe a five-year direction, and four hours later a procurement clerk in Kolhapur would open an envelope and read a table of dates as a contract. Deepa had until then to decide what kind of document she was actually writing, and for whom — and she was no longer sure the company had ever asked itself that question, or that anyone would thank her for asking it now.

Strategy, Roadmap, Plan: What the Three-Layer Ladder Gets Right, and Where It Quietly Inverts

Two product leaders, one in connected hardware and one in regulated payments, discover in the same fortnight of February 2026 that the layer of their document stack which was supposed to be the most disposable is in fact the most irreversible — and that the neat ladder they had been taught describes the wrong variable.

The argument of this page. The familiar ladder — vision above strategy, strategy above roadmap, roadmap above plan — is usually taught as a hierarchy of abstraction: each rung down is more detailed, more dated, more disposable. That reading is serviceable for a pure software business with short supply chains and no third-party dates, and it is what a competent practitioner carries around.

An expert carries something else. The three layers are not three zoom levels on the same object. They are three different kinds of information — a forgone alternative, a sequencing logic, and a named capacity commitment — and the ladder holds together only so long as the cost of changing your mind falls monotonically as you descend it. In hardware, in regulated markets, in enterprise contracts, in marketplaces below liquidity, and in AI products whose key inputs arrive exogenously, that monotonicity breaks. The plan hardens before the roadmap is written; the roadmap becomes the binding contract; the strategy becomes the layer that flexes. Mature companies handle this, but not in the way their published process documents claim. They keep a second book.

Whether that second book is a healthy adaptation or an admission that the framework is wrong is a live disagreement in the field, and this page does not resolve it.

1. Two decisions, one fortnight

On the evening of 9 February 2026, Divya Ramaswami sat in a conference room above a contract-manufacturing floor in Vatva, on the eastern industrial edge of Ahmedabad, looking at a quotation for injection-mould tooling. The number was ₹1.08 crore. The lead time printed beside it, in a smaller font, was twenty-two weeks.

Ramaswami, forty-one, had been Chief Product Officer at Yashomati Devices for nineteen months. Yashomati sold cold-chain integrity to Indian pharmaceutical distributors and dairy processors: a battery-powered temperature-and-humidity logger roughly the size of a matchbox, clipped inside a shipment carton or a reefer van, and a SaaS platform that turned the loggers' uploads into excursion alerts, audit trails against the record-keeping expectations distributors face under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, and claims evidence when a consignment spoiled. Revenue for the year ending March 2026 would land near ₹64 crore, of which roughly ₹41 crore was device hardware sold at a gross margin of 28 percent and ₹23 crore was software subscription at 81 percent. The board — two financial investors and a strategic investor from a logistics group — had spent the last three quarterly meetings pressing the same question in different words: was Yashomati a device company with a dashboard, or a data company that happened to ship devices?

Ramaswami had scheduled the answer for the annual strategy review on 21 April 2026. The tooling quotation, sitting in front of her in February, made that date a fiction. The mould in question was for a next-generation logger with an onboard cellular radio and eighteen months of battery life, which was the physical precondition for Yashomati owning the sensing layer rather than integrating with whatever logger a customer's freight forwarder happened to use. Twenty-two weeks of tooling lead time, stacked on a sixteen-week bill-of-materials freeze that had to precede it, and a BIS registration slot under MeitY's Compulsory Registration Scheme plus a wireless type-approval that together consumed fourteen weeks and could not be booked speculatively, meant that a decision made in late April would not produce a shippable device before the following March. If Yashomati intended to have the new logger in the field for the 2027 monsoon — the season when cold-chain failures peak and when procurement committees at distributors actually move — the purchase order had to go out by the first week of March 2026.

The strategic question, in other words, had to be answered seven weeks before the strategy review that existed to answer it. What Ramaswami had been calling her plan — the quarterly, sprint-scoped, engineer-assigned layer that every textbook describes as the most disposable rung on the ladder — was about to make the least reversible decision in the company's history. And her roadmap, a tidy Now / Next / Later board reviewed every quarter, said nothing about it, because tooling is not a feature.

Three days later and eight hundred kilometres south, on 12 February, Nikhil Bhattacharya faced a structurally different version of the same problem. Bhattacharya, thirty-six, was VP Product at Yugantar Payments, a Bengaluru company holding a payment-aggregator authorisation from the Reserve Bank of India and processing, in January 2026, an annualised total payment volume of about ₹9,400 crore across roughly 214,000 small merchants — kirana stores, salons, clinics, tuition centres — at a blended take rate of 0.42 percent, for revenue near ₹39 crore. Yugantar also ran a thin consumer side: a payments app with 1.9 million monthly active users whose only real reason to exist was to make Yugantar's merchant acceptance network more valuable than a commodity QR sticker.

Bhattacharya's board had asked for a four-quarter roadmap. He had sat down to write it and discovered that he could not, for two reasons that had nothing to do with effort. The first was that his compliance backlog — work flowing from the RBI's payment-aggregator framework and from the succession of NPCI circulars that govern interoperability on UPI — consumed, on his engineering director's estimate, 41 percent of the platform team's capacity for the next two quarters, against dates set by someone who did not work at Yugantar and would not be negotiating. The second was subtler. The remaining 59 percent was contested between the merchant side and the consumer side, and the right answer depended on a variable that was not a date. Yugantar's consumer app only became strategically load-bearing above a merchant acceptance density of roughly one participating merchant per 900 residents in a given pincode cluster — the point at which a consumer could reasonably expect the app to work at the next shop rather than the third one. Fourteen of Yugantar's forty-one active clusters were above that line in January. The rest were not, and whether they crossed it in Q2 or Q4 depended on field-sales productivity, not on the calendar.

A four-quarter roadmap with themes assigned to quarters would therefore be a lie in both directions: precise where Bhattacharya had no control, and vague where he had real knowledge. What he wanted to write was a roadmap whose gates were states rather than dates. What his board wanted to read was a grid with four columns.

Ramaswami's problem was that the bottom rung of her ladder had become the top. Bhattacharya's was that the middle rung was being asked to carry a time axis the world would not supply. Neither problem is exotic, and neither is well handled by the ladder as it is usually taught.

2. What the three layers actually are, and where they came from

Begin with definitions sharper than the working ones. The useful discriminator is not abstraction and not time horizon. It is the type of proposition each document asserts.

A strategy asserts a forgone alternative. Its irreducible content is a choice with a named thing given up: a segment not served, a competitor not fought, a capability deliberately rented rather than owned. A document that contains no sentence of the form "and therefore not X" is not a strategy; it is an ambition. This is the discriminating test, and it is stricter than it sounds, because most documents titled strategy contain only positive assertions.

A roadmap asserts a sequencing logic under uncertainty: a claim that doing A before B produces more value, or buys more information, than doing B before A, together with the reason. Its irreducible content is the ordering argument, not the items. Strip the items out and keep the argument and you still have a roadmap; strip the argument out and keep the items and you have a list.

A plan asserts a named capacity commitment: these people, this much of their time, against this scope, by this date, with this person accountable. Its irreducible content is the fact that somebody's name can be attached to the shortfall.

Notice that these three are logically independent. A document can assert a forgone alternative without any sequencing logic (a strategy with no roadmap). It can assert a sequencing logic without any forgone alternative (the very common roadmap-on-nothing). It can assert capacity commitments without either (a beautifully resourced plan executing an unexamined assumption). The ladder metaphor implies that the lower rungs are derived from the upper ones. In practice they are three independent assertions that a healthy organisation makes consistent with each other, which is a much weaker and much more honest claim.

The intellectual history, briefly but properly

The three words arrived from three unrelated traditions, which is why they sit so awkwardly together.

Plan is the oldest and the most industrially mature. Henry Gantt's bar charts, developed around the First World War for munitions scheduling, and the Program Evaluation and Review Technique built for the US Navy's Polaris submarine programme in 1958, gave the world a rigorous formalism for scheduling interdependent work under resource constraints. Nearly everything a modern product organisation does at the plan layer — critical path, float, resource levelling, earned value — descends from that lineage, and the lineage has one built-in assumption worth naming: that the content of the work is settled and the problem is execution.

Strategy, in the corporate sense, arrives through Alfred Chandler's Strategy and Structure (1962) and then Igor Ansoff's Corporate Strategy (1965), which fused strategy with the long-range-planning apparatus of the era: multi-year forecasts, gap analysis, planning departments. The most important event in the field was the repudiation of that fusion. Henry Mintzberg's The Rise and Fall of Strategic Planning (1994) argued, with a great deal of field evidence, that planning is not a method for producing strategy — planning is analysis, strategy-making is synthesis, and an organisation that confuses the two will reliably produce elaborate plans in service of unexamined premises. Mintzberg and James Waters had already, in 1985, split realised strategy into a deliberate component and an emergent one, and observed that the emergent share is usually larger than executives admit.

Roadmap is the youngest and, revealingly, did not begin in product management at all. It begins in semiconductor R&D: Motorola's technology-roadmapping process, described publicly by Charles Willyard and Cheryl McClees in 1987 and championed by Robert Galvin, was a mechanism for aligning long-lead technology development with product generations across a decade. Robert Phaal, Clare Farrukh and David Probert at the Cambridge Institute for Manufacturing later generalised it into the T-Plan framework. The original object was explicitly about lead time: the roadmap existed because a process technology took eight years and a product generation took two, and somebody needed a picture that made the mismatch visible. When product management borrowed the word in the 2000s and 2010s, it kept the picture and discarded the lead-time problem the picture was invented to solve. Much of what follows in this page is an argument for putting that problem back.

The schools, and the specific propositions each will and will not sign

Four positions are genuinely held by serious people. They are not compatible.

The deliberate-design school, running from Porter through Rumelt, holds that strategy is a diagnosis and a set of coherent, consciously chosen actions, and that the roadmap and plan are its faithful translations. It will sign: "a company without a written, choice-bearing strategy is worse off than one with a mediocre written strategy." It will not sign: "the resource allocation pattern is the strategy, whatever the document says."

The emergence school, running from Mintzberg through Robert Burgelman's process research, holds the reverse. Burgelman's study of Intel's exit from dynamic memory — published in 1994 as Fading Memories — documented that Intel's middle managers, allocating scarce fab capacity by a standing rule of margin per wafer start, had shifted silicon from DRAM to microprocessors years before Gordon Moore and Andrew Grove formally decided to leave the memory business. The exit was executed by the capacity plan and only later ratified as strategy. This school will sign: "if you want to know a company's strategy, read its capacity allocation, not its strategy deck." It will not sign: "the roadmap is derived from the strategy."

The communication school — associated in product management with Now / Next / Later formats and with the argument that a roadmap's primary consumer is a stakeholder rather than a builder — holds that the roadmap is fundamentally a device for managing expectations across an organisational boundary, and should be designed for that job. It will sign: "a roadmap that is internally rigorous and externally illegible has failed." It will not sign: "the roadmap is a planning instrument."

The abolitionist school — Basecamp's Shape Up, with its six-week cycles and explicit refusal to maintain a roadmap, and the continuous-discovery tradition in its stronger forms — holds that the roadmap layer is the source of most product dysfunction, because a published sequence becomes a commitment and a commitment destroys the option to learn. It will sign: "the correct number of roadmap items beyond the current cycle is zero." It will not sign: "a roadmap can be non-binding if you label it non-binding" — its whole point is that labels do not survive contact with a sales organisation.

Ramaswami's situation is a direct test of the deliberate-design school, because her tooling lead time forces a resource commitment ahead of the deliberation. Bhattacharya's is a direct test of the communication school, because his board's demand for four columns is a demand about legibility that conflicts with what he knows.

3. The mechanics, worked: commitment lead time as the governing variable

Expert practice turns on a quantity that most process documentation never names. Call it the commitment lead time, L: for a given decision, the interval between making it and the point at which reversing it costs more than the expected value of the change. And call R the revision period of the document layer that owns the decision — how often that layer is legitimately re-opened. Two weeks for a sprint plan; a quarter for a roadmap; a year or two for a strategy.

The single most useful test an expert applies is the comparison of L to R.

If L > R, the decision hardens before the layer that owns it next meets. That layer's reviews are theatre: they discuss decisions that are already made.

This is not a metaphor; it is an arithmetic condition, and it produces the diagram below.

Figure 1 — The separability frontier. Every point above the dashed line is a commitment that outlives the review cadence of the document layer nominally responsible for it. In a pure software business almost every point sits comfortably below the line, which is why the three-layer ladder feels natural there. Yashomati's two defining decisions — tooling and certification — sit above it, as does every regulated mandate in Bhattacharya's backlog.

The second-order effect is the one that matters. When a decision sits above the frontier, organisations do not usually notice and correct. They notice and relabel. The tooling decision gets discussed at the quarterly roadmap review as though it were open, a decision is recorded, and the procurement team — who ordered the mould in March because the factory slot required it — quietly executes what was already true. Over two or three cycles this trains everyone in the room that roadmap reviews do not change anything, which is precisely the cynicism that makes the next genuinely open decision get treated as foregone as well.

The step everyone leaves implicit: the reversal-cost ratio

Lead time alone is insufficient, because some long-lead commitments are cheap to abandon. The refinement is the reversal-cost ratio, ρ = (cost already sunk plus cost to unwind) ÷ (total cost of the original commitment). An item with ρ below roughly 0.15 remains a genuine roadmap item however long its lead time, because walking away is nearly free. An item above roughly 0.4 is functionally a plan commitment on the day it is initiated, whatever column it occupies.

The formal treatment that does exist, and its limits

There is a respectable quantitative apparatus for sequencing decisions: Don Reinertsen's cost of delay divided by duration, usually written CD3, which ranks work by economic urgency per unit of capacity consumed. It is genuinely useful at the roadmap layer, and it is worth working one instance to see both its power and its boundary.

Bhattacharya scored his three discretionary Q2 candidates. Merchant settlement-speed improvement: estimated ₹1.9 crore of annualised gross profit at risk to competitive churn, arriving linearly, so cost of delay ≈ ₹15.8 lakh per month; duration 2.5 months; CD3 = 6.3. Consumer app rewards revamp: ₹0.9 crore at stake, ₹7.5 lakh per month, duration 1.5 months, CD3 = 5.0. Merchant lending-partner integration: ₹3.4 crore of new revenue, but it cannot begin earning until a partner bank's own release train in Q3, so its cost of delay for the first three months is approximately zero and only then rises to ₹28 lakh per month; duration 3 months; CD3 over the relevant window = 9.3, but only if started no earlier than mid-Q2, because starting earlier buys nothing.

The ranking that falls out — lending integration, then settlement speed, then rewards — is defensible and would not have been produced by intuition. But note what CD3 cannot see. It has no representation for the fact that the rewards revamp is only worth doing in clusters above the acceptance-density threshold, and that the number of such clusters is itself a function of whether settlement speed improves, because faster settlement is the single strongest driver of field-sales conversion. The dependency is not a schedule dependency, which CD3 handles; it is a state dependency, which it does not. This is the precise point at which the quantitative treatment runs out and judgement resumes, and an expert knows where that line is rather than either worshipping the model or ignoring it.

4. When the ladder applies, and when it actively misleads

State the conditions as claims that can be checked, and apply each to both protagonists.

Claim 1: the ladder holds when revision periods are separated by a factor of at least three. Strategy at 52–104 weeks, roadmap at 13–26, plan at 1–3 gives ratios of roughly 4:1 and 8:1, and the layers can behave independently. Compress any adjacent pair below about 2:1 and the boundary becomes fictional — people simply maintain two documents that always change together, which is pure overhead. Yashomati fails this test on the roadmap-to-plan boundary: the effective revision period of a plan whose central item has a 22-week lead time is not two weeks but twenty-two, which sits inside the roadmap's own band. Yugantar passes it on paper and fails it in the half of capacity that is mandated, where the plan and the roadmap have the same exogenous date and there is nothing to separate.

Figure 2 — On the left, the cadences of the three layers occupy disjoint bands, and each can change without forcing the others. On the right, the plan's effective revision period — set by tooling, certification and mandate lead times rather than by the sprint calendar — moves left to right into the roadmap's band. Inside the shaded zone the two documents necessarily move together, and maintaining them separately produces ritual rather than information.

Claim 2: the ladder holds when the organisation controls the dates. If a third party sets a date you cannot move — a regulator, a partner bank's release train, a retailer's planogram reset, a festive-season demand peak — then that date is a constraint at the plan layer that propagates upward, and the correct mental model is not a ladder but a fixed point with everything else arranged around it. Yugantar fails this test outright for 41 percent of capacity. Yashomati fails it seasonally: the 2027 monsoon is not a date Yashomati chose.

Claim 3: the ladder holds when the roadmap is not contractually binding. The moment a roadmap item appears in an enterprise contract's schedule, a master service agreement, or a renewal term sheet, it has acquired a plan's accountability without a plan's resourcing discipline. Yashomati has three such items with two large pharmaceutical distributors. Yugantar has none, because its merchants are too small to negotiate, which is one of the underappreciated freedoms of a long-tail business.

Claim 4: the ladder holds when progress is time-paced rather than state-paced. Shona Brown and Kathleen Eisenhardt's 1998 distinction between time pacing — transitions triggered by the calendar — and event pacing — transitions triggered by something happening in the world — maps directly onto this. Roadmaps with quarterly columns are a time-pacing instrument. A marketplace below liquidity, a hardware product awaiting a certification, and an AI product awaiting a model capability are all event-paced, and forcing them into columns encodes a false claim. Bhattacharya fails this test on the consumer side and passes it on the merchant side, which is exactly why his single four-column grid could not be made honest.

Where the ladder is actively misleading, rather than merely inapplicable, is the case that deserves emphasis: a company whose real strategy is being made at the plan layer, by capacity allocation, while an unread strategy document provides false comfort that the question has been settled elsewhere. This is Burgelman's Intel finding as a pathology rather than a curiosity. Yashomati was three weeks from living it.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

Multi-product portfolios and the seam problem

In a single-product company the three layers are three documents. In a five-product company they are three documents per product plus one portfolio layer, and the interesting failures all occur at the seams. The characteristic seam pathology is that the roadmap becomes the negotiation surface, for a structural reason: strategy is too abstract to argue with productively, and plans are too concrete — arguing with a plan means arguing with a named engineer's estimate, which is socially expensive. The roadmap is the only layer that is simultaneously public and unfalsifiable, so all the political energy in the organisation collects there.

Yugm Commerce Cloud, a Hyderabad company selling order management, warehouse management and a returns product to mid-market retailers, discovered this at a scale of 240 engineers across three product lines. Its portfolio roadmap review ran four hours a month and consisted almost entirely of product leaders trading sequence positions. Its strategy document had not been re-opened in fourteen months. Its plan layer was excellent. The company was, in Mintzberg's terms, all deliberate-planning apparatus and no strategy-making, and the tell was that no portfolio review in a year had resulted in anything being cancelled — only reordered. Reordering without cancellation is the reliable signature of a roadmap doing political work rather than analytical work.

Two-sided markets: the state-gated roadmap

Bhattacharya's problem has a known solution shape that is under-taught. Where the strategic logic is state-dependent, the roadmap should be written as a set of gated branches, with each gate specified as a measurable threshold and a named owner who declares the gate passed. The calendar then appears only as an expectation, clearly marked as such, rather than as the structure of the document.

Figure 3 — The same quarter's work expressed as a time-gated grid and as a state-gated branch structure. The second is harder to put on a board slide and strictly more truthful. The discipline that makes it work is naming a gate owner: a threshold nobody is accountable for declaring will never be declared.

The objection to state gating is real and should be stated: boards and finance functions need a date to budget against, and "when the clusters cross density" cannot be entered into a cash-flow model. The mature practice is not to choose but to publish both, with the state-gated version as the primary document and a dated expectation layer attached, explicitly labelled as a forecast with a stated confidence. Bhattacharya's eventual draft carried a line under each branch reading, for example, "expected Q3 FY27, 60 percent confidence, based on current cluster crossing rate of 2.1 per month."

Regulated products

In a regulated business, part of the roadmap is written by somebody else, and the error practitioners make is treating that part as a tax to be minimised rather than as strategy to be shaped. The expert move is to notice that mandated work is a capability investment whose strategic value depends entirely on how you build it. Yugantar could satisfy its interoperability obligations with the minimum conforming implementation, or it could build the same obligations as a reusable compliance-evidence service that would later let it sell to larger merchants who demand audit artefacts. Same mandate, same date, same cost within perhaps 15 percent — and one of the two options is strategic and the other is not.

Hardware plus software

Yashomati's case generalises. Where a product has an atoms component, the layers must be maintained on two different clocks that are then reconciled, rather than on one. Mature hardware-software companies run what is sometimes called a dual-cadence structure: a hardware programme plan on an eighteen-to-twenty-four-month cycle with formal gates borrowed from stage-gate development, and a software roadmap on a quarterly cycle, with an explicit reconciliation artefact listing every point at which a software commitment depends on a hardware decision that has already hardened. The crucial and rarely-documented discipline is that the reconciliation artefact runs in both directions: it also lists the software options that the hardware freeze has closed off, so that the cost of the freeze is visible rather than absorbed silently.

AI-native products

Yatnik Labs, a Bengaluru company building an AI agent that handles tier-one customer operations for Indian consumer-internet companies, illustrates the newest version of the problem. Its roadmap contained items whose feasibility depended on capabilities that would arrive from foundation-model providers on a schedule Yatnik neither knew nor influenced. Committing to build a workaround had a cost; waiting had a cost; and the expected values were genuinely close.

Work one instance. Yatnik's multi-step refund-negotiation flow required reliable tool use across seven sequential calls. In February 2026 its incumbent model achieved this in 71 percent of evaluation cases; the product needed 93 percent. Building a deterministic scaffold to close the gap was estimated at 11 engineer-weeks, with an expected life of two to three model generations before it became dead weight to maintain and remove — call the removal and interim maintenance cost 4 engineer-weeks. Waiting for a model generation that closed the gap natively was estimated, from the previous four release intervals of 19, 23, 14 and 21 weeks, at a median of 20 weeks. The revenue at stake was ₹62 lakh of annualised contract value from two prospects who had named the flow as a condition of signing.

The expected-value arithmetic: building costs 15 engineer-weeks all-in (≈ ₹18 lakh fully loaded) and secures ₹62 lakh with high probability. Waiting costs approximately ₹24 lakh of delayed revenue over the 20-week median wait, with perhaps a 35 percent chance that the two prospects walk entirely, adding an expected ₹22 lakh of loss. Build wins, and not narrowly. But the second-order point is the one Yatnik's head of product, Ira Sundaram, actually made in the review: the correct roadmap entry was not "build the scaffold" but "build the scaffold and schedule its removal review for the second model release from now" — a roadmap item with a built-in expiry, which is a construction the standard Now / Next / Later grammar has no way to express. AI-native roadmaps need a fourth column that most tools do not offer: Retire.

6. Nine distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

i. The roadmap is an observer-effect instrument, not a passive description

A competent practitioner treats the roadmap as a representation of intent. An expert knows that publishing it changes the intent. The moment a theme appears on a shared roadmap, a sales engineer quotes it on a call, a customer-success manager anchors a renewal conversation on it, a candidate accepts an offer partly because of it, and a partner sequences their own work against it. Each of those is a small commitment that raises the reversal cost of the item, so that a roadmap entry which was a 0.05-ρ bet in January can be a 0.45-ρ obligation by March without a single engineering hour having been spent. The tell: when someone proposes dropping a Later item and three functions object on grounds unrelated to the item's merit, the roadmap has been doing commitment work behind your back. The obvious reading — that the objectors are being political — is usually wrong; they are correctly reporting commitments the roadmap created.

ii. A strategy that survives an entire year unchanged may be strong, or it may be unread

Stability is the conventional virtue of the strategy layer, and it is genuinely a virtue. But there are two ways for a document not to change: because it keeps being right, and because nobody consults it. These are indistinguishable from the outside and trivially distinguishable from the inside. The tell: ask how many times in the last year the strategy document was cited to refuse something. A strategy that has never been used to say no in twelve months is not stable; it is inert. Yugm Commerce Cloud's fourteen-month-old document had a citation count, when someone finally checked the meeting notes, of two — both in slide decks, neither in a decision.

iii. Cancellation rate is the health metric, not delivery rate

Competent organisations measure roadmap health by the proportion of committed items delivered. Experts also watch the proportion cancelled, and know that a cancellation rate near zero is bad news. If a roadmap represents genuine bets under uncertainty, some of those bets must lose, and losing must be visible. A plausible healthy band, across the companies where this has been examined carefully, is somewhere between 10 and 25 percent of roadmap items cancelled or radically rescoped per year. The tell: a roadmap where items never die but simply migrate rightward, quarter after quarter. The obvious reading is under-capacity. The real reading is usually that the organisation has no mechanism for admitting a bet was wrong, so it expresses the admission as perpetual deferral, which costs more because the item continues to consume planning attention.

iv. "We are behind on the roadmap" is almost always a mis-description

You cannot be behind on a roadmap, because a roadmap makes no date commitment; you can only be behind on a plan, or wrong about a sequencing logic. When a senior leader says the roadmap has slipped, an expert asks which of the two they mean, because the remedies are opposite. Behind on the plan means an execution or estimation problem and calls for capacity, scope or date adjustment. Wrong about the sequence means the ordering argument has been falsified by evidence and calls for re-deriving the roadmap from the strategy. Treating the second as the first — adding engineers to accelerate work whose premise has collapsed — is among the most expensive errors in the discipline. The tell: the proposed remedy is always resourcing, never re-argument.

v. Strategy exists at several altitudes, and the same sentence can be strategy at one and a roadmap item at another

This is the most common source of unproductive meetings. "Own the sensing layer" is a genuine strategic choice at Yashomati's product-line altitude — it forgoes a partner-integration business — and is simultaneously a roadmap theme relative to the corporate-level choice to be a cold-chain company rather than a general industrial-IoT company. The tell: two competent people arguing about whether something "belongs in the strategy or on the roadmap" and neither of them naming an altitude. The resolution is not to decide who is right but to ask each of them what the alternative they are forgoing is; if their answers name different scopes, they are at different altitudes and were never disagreeing.

vi. The plan's estimate distribution matters more than its estimate

Competent planners produce point estimates and pad them. Experts care about the shape. A plan built from twelve items each estimated with roughly symmetric uncertainty behaves very differently from one built from twelve items of which one has a long right tail — an integration with an external partner, a migration with unknown data quality, a certification. In the second case the aggregate is dominated by the single tail item, and adding buffer uniformly across the twelve is a waste; the buffer belongs almost entirely on the one. The tell: a plan whose buffer is expressed as a single percentage applied to the total. The obvious reading is prudence; it is actually a failure to look at where the variance lives.

vii. The roadmap's most informative section is the one naming what it excludes

This is widely repeated as advice and rarely done well, because the hard part is not listing exclusions but listing the credible ones. A "not now" list containing items nobody wanted is decoration. A useful exclusion list names the three things a reasonable person inside the company actively advocated for and did not get, with the reason. The tell: read the exclusion list and ask whether any named person is disappointed by it. If nobody is, it is not an exclusion list; it is a list of things that were never going to happen anyway.

viii. OKRs sit between strategy and roadmap, and their characteristic failure is measuring the plan

The bridge function of objectives and key results is well understood in principle: the objective restates a strategic intent, the key results measure whether the roadmap themes are producing the outcome the strategy predicted. The characteristic corruption is that key results drift downward into plan-layer output measures, because those are easy to count and always achievable. "Ship the new onboarding flow by 30 June" is a plan milestone masquerading as a key result. The tell: a key result that is fully within the team's control. A genuine key result should be achievable only if a hypothesis about the world turns out to be true; if the team can guarantee it by working hard, it is measuring effort, not learning.

ix. Every organisation above roughly 150 people keeps two books, and pretending otherwise is the problem

There is the published roadmap — for customers, sales, the board, recruiting — and there is the internal commitment ledger that engineering leadership actually runs against. Experts know both exist, keep the divergence measured, and treat divergence above a threshold as an incident. Competent practitioners either deny the second book exists or let it drift unmeasured. The tell: ask a senior engineer and a senior account executive, separately, what the team is working on this quarter, and compare. A divergence of 10 to 20 percent is ordinary translation loss. Beyond 40 percent, the published roadmap has become a marketing artefact with a product manager's name on it, and somebody will discover this at a renewal.

8. Three worked examples

Example one: Yashomati handles an inversion well

Having built the commitment register in Table 1, Ramaswami did something the ladder does not describe. She moved the strategy review from 21 April to 27 February, and narrowed it to a single question: is Yashomati willing to be a device company whose software is a differentiator, or a software company whose devices are a distribution mechanism? She did not pretend the roadmap would decide it, because the tooling PO would.

The arithmetic she brought was a five-year contribution comparison. Owning the sensing layer: device gross margin 28 percent on an expected 2027–28 volume of 240,000 units at ₹1,850 average selling price gives ₹124 crore of revenue and ₹34.7 crore of gross profit, plus attach-rate-driven software revenue of roughly ₹38 crore at 81 percent, total gross profit ₹65.5 crore, against ₹3.15 crore of incremental commitment and an estimated ₹9 crore of ongoing hardware programme overhead. Renting the sensing layer: no device revenue, software revenue of perhaps ₹52 crore because third-party ingestion opens accounts Yashomati cannot reach with its own hardware, gross profit ₹42 crore, overhead ₹2 crore, and — the decisive term — a dependency on logger vendors who could integrate a dashboard themselves within eighteen months.

The numbers favoured owning by roughly ₹12 crore of five-year gross profit, which Ramaswami correctly described to the board as inside the error bars. The decision turned on the dependency term, not the arithmetic. What made the process good was not that the answer was right but that the question was asked seven weeks earlier than the calendar said, because someone had computed L and noticed.

Example two: Yugantar makes a partial recovery

Bhattacharya's state-gated draft went to the board on 3 March 2026 and was received badly. The finance director could not model it. The compromise that emerged over two further sessions is instructive precisely because it is not clean: Yugantar publishes a four-column grid in which columns one and two are genuine dated plans (mandate work, plus settlement speed, both fully resourced) and columns three and four are explicitly labelled "gated — expected timing only," with the gate condition printed in the cell. The board accepted it. The field-sales organisation, which had previously treated the consumer roadmap as a promise, began reporting cluster density weekly because a gate depended on it — a second-order benefit nobody predicted, and arguably worth more than the roadmap change itself. Measurement follows accountability far more reliably than accountability follows measurement.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Disagreement one: is the strategy document causal, or is it a rationalisation of the capacity plan?

The deliberate position, steelmanned: organisations that write choice-bearing strategies allocate capacity differently from those that do not, and the difference is observable in what they refuse. The evidence is largely case-based but consistent: the discipline of naming a forgone alternative forces conflicts into the open at a point when they are cheap to resolve, whereas emergent allocation resolves them silently and late, at the level of individual managers optimising locally. For this to be wrong, it would have to be true that written strategies do not change allocation patterns — a claim that could be tested, and rarely is.

The emergent position, steelmanned: Burgelman's Intel evidence is not an anecdote; it is a process study showing that the firm's most consequential strategic act was performed by a resource-allocation rule and ratified afterward. Generalise it and the implication is stark: the capacity plan is the strategy, expressed in the only currency that binds, and the strategy document is at best a communication device and at worst a source of false confidence that a question has been settled. For this to be wrong, there would have to be cases where a written strategy demonstrably redirected allocation against the grain of local incentives — and proponents of the deliberate view have not, on the whole, produced them in a form that survives scrutiny.

Note that the two positions generate opposite advice for Ramaswami. The first says: hold the strategy review properly, write the choice down, then let the tooling decision follow. The second says: the tooling PO is the strategy, so stop writing and start negotiating the PO's terms — for instance, buying an option on a factory slot rather than the slot itself. Ramaswami, in the event, did both, which is common and is not a synthesis; it is two incompatible theories being hedged against.

Disagreement two: should a roadmap carry dates at all?

The no-dates position: dates on a roadmap are read as commitments regardless of disclaimers, and the observer effect of distinction (i) means they will acquire real reversal costs. Since the roadmap's job is sequencing logic, dates add nothing it needs and import everything it should avoid. Now / Next / Later exists precisely to give ordering without duration. For this to be wrong, it would have to be the case that organisations can in fact hold an undated sequence without stakeholders inventing dates for it — and the honest observation is that many cannot.

The dated position: in enterprise software, procurement cycles, budget years and integration windows mean a customer genuinely cannot act on an undated sequence, and refusing dates does not eliminate the commitment, it just moves it into a private conversation between an account executive and a customer where product has no visibility. Better a published date with a stated confidence than an unpublished one with none. For this to be wrong, it would have to be true that private commitments are no worse than public ones — and Yugm's experience argues the opposite.

Disagreement three: is OKR the right bridge between strategy and roadmap?

In favour: the bridge problem is real — something must translate a forgone alternative into a measurable prediction — and the objective-plus-key-results form is the only widely adopted mechanism that does it without becoming a third planning document. Against: in practice OKRs cascade, and cascading converts them into exactly the plan-layer output measures distinction (viii) warns about, so the mechanism reliably decays into the thing it was meant to prevent. The strongest version of the sceptical case is not that OKRs are wrong but that the quarterly cadence of OKRs mismatches both the strategy layer above and the plan layer below, sitting on a clock that belongs to neither. Nobody in the field has a good answer to that objection.

Disagreement four: is the roadmap layer necessary at all?

The abolitionist case deserves its strongest statement. If strategy supplies the choice and the plan supplies the commitment, the roadmap's unique contribution is sequencing logic — and sequencing logic could equally be a paragraph inside the strategy, re-derived each cycle, with no standing document to become a contract. Basecamp's six-week cycles operate this way and the company is not obviously worse for it. The counter is scale-dependent: below a hundred people the sequencing argument can live in someone's head and be re-told; above it, the cost of re-telling exceeds the cost of maintaining a document, and the roadmap earns its place as a communication instrument even if it earns nothing as a planning one. What neither camp has shown is where exactly that crossover sits, or whether it is a function of headcount at all rather than of the number of organisational boundaries the sequence must cross.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this correctly identifies documents. Someone who has internalised it does five things differently, and they are observable.

They ask for lead times before they ask for estimates. The first question an expert asks of a quarter's candidate work is not "how big is it" but "when does it stop being reversible," because that determines which conversation it belongs in. A competent practitioner sizes; an expert sequences by reversibility first and size second.

They keep a commitment ledger that is not any of the three documents. It lists forward-looking statements — to customers, partners, candidates, the board — with dates, sources and reversal costs, and it is reconciled on a fixed cadence. This artefact appears in no framework and in most well-run companies above a few hundred people.

They are comfortable letting a document be one thing and not another. A strategy with no dates and no features is not incomplete; a plan with no strategic reasoning is not shallow. The instinct to make every document complete is the instinct that produces the forty-slide deck which is simultaneously all three and useful as none.

They notice the direction of causation in their own organisation. Asked whether their strategy drives their capacity plan or the reverse, they answer with evidence — a specific instance in the last two quarters — rather than with the org chart. Most people answer with the org chart.

Finally, they treat disagreement about which layer a thing belongs to as diagnostic rather than annoying. When two capable colleagues cannot agree whether an item is strategy or roadmap, an expert reads it as a signal that the altitudes are unclear or that the item's reversibility is not understood, and goes looking for the underlying ambiguity instead of arbitrating the label.

12. What each of them decided

Ramaswami issued the tooling purchase order on 6 March 2026, three days later than the factory had asked, having spent the intervening week negotiating a change: Yashomati paid an additional ₹9 lakh for a slot reservation that could be converted to a full order as late as 3 April, which bought her three weeks of genuine optionality for 8.3 percent of the tooling cost. She held the narrowed strategy review on 27 February, got the board to state the owning-versus-renting choice explicitly, and recorded the decision — own the sensing layer — with its forgone alternative written in one sentence: Yashomati would not pursue the third-party-logger integration business in FY27, accepting that this ceded roughly ₹14 crore of addressable software revenue to competitors. Her reasoning was that the arithmetic was within its own error bars and the tiebreaker was structural dependency, which is a strategic consideration rather than a financial one. She also instituted the commitment register of Table 1 as a standing monthly artefact, which is the change most likely to matter in three years.

Bhattacharya published the hybrid grid on 17 March 2026: two dated, funded columns and two gated ones with named gate owners and stated confidences. He did not get what he thought was right, and he said so in the document, in a short paragraph explaining why columns three and four could not honestly carry dates. The paragraph was, in the end, the most-quoted part of the roadmap, mostly by field-sales managers explaining to merchants why something had not shipped. Whether that counts as the communication school vindicating itself or the abolitionist school scoring a point about published sequences is a matter on which reasonable people at Yugantar still differ.

Discussion questions

  1. Ramaswami paid ₹9 lakh — 8.3 percent of the tooling cost — to move a decision three weeks later. Under what conditions is buying optionality at the plan layer a better use of money than improving the quality of the strategic analysis itself? Compute what Yashomati's decision quality would have to improve by to justify spending the same ₹9 lakh on analysis instead.
  2. Yugm's recovery introduced a fourth artefact rather than fixing the roadmap. Is the commitment register evidence that the three-layer model is incomplete, or evidence that Yugm's roadmap discipline was simply poor? What observation would distinguish the two explanations?
  3. Bhattacharya's field-sales organisation began measuring cluster density weekly only because a roadmap gate depended on it. If the choice of what a roadmap gates on determines what an organisation measures, does that make gate selection a strategic act — and if so, which of the four schools in section 2 can best account for it?

13. Going deeper

Product vision and mission
The layer above all three, and the only one whose job is to outlive several strategies. Worth revisiting because a vision specific enough to be mistaken for a strategy is the commonest upstream cause of the confusions on this page; it unlocks the ability to change strategy without the organisation reading it as a loss of direction.
Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later
The concrete format most often used to express sequencing without dates, and the natural place to work through the state-gating problem of section 5. It unlocks the practical question of what belongs in Later and how a Later item is allowed to die.
The roadmap as communication
Directly addresses the observer effect of distinction (i) and the two-book divergence of Yugm's failure. It unlocks the discipline of designing different roadmap renderings for different audiences without letting them diverge in substance.
OKRs and goal setting
The contested bridge of disagreement three. Worth studying next because the characteristic corruption — key results that measure plan output — is the single most common way the link between strategy and roadmap silently breaks. It unlocks a measurable test of whether a roadmap theme is doing what the strategy predicted.
Annual and quarterly planning
Where the cadence question of Figure 2 becomes an operating calendar, and where the mismatch between a financial year and a product's natural rhythm has to be resolved in practice. It unlocks the negotiation with finance that most product organisations handle badly.
Capacity planning
The layer at which, on Burgelman's reading, strategy is actually made. Essential next reading precisely because if the emergent school is right, this is the most strategic document in the company. It unlocks the ability to test, empirically, which school your own organisation belongs to.
Dependency management
The mechanics behind the lead times that drive the whole argument of this page, including the distinction between schedule dependencies, which planning tools model well, and state dependencies, which they do not. It unlocks the reconciliation artefact that dual-cadence hardware and software organisations depend on.

Strategy vs Roadmap vs Plan

Is this document a strategy, a roadmap, or a plan — and does it know? A close read of one bad board meeting at a Bengaluru manufacturing-software company, and the discipline that keeps the three from collapsing into each other.

1. A board meeting in Bengaluru

On the morning of 14 October 2025, Ananya Deshmukh, VP of Product at Parisar Analytics, opened her laptop forty minutes before the company's board meeting and read, for the third time, the slide she was about to present. It was titled "Product Strategy FY26," and it consisted of a Jira export: forty-one rows, each with a feature name, a target quarter, and a coloured dot for status. Predictive maintenance alerts. Multi-tenant dashboard theming. SAP connector v2. Mobile push notifications. The dots were mostly amber.

Parisar Analytics sold shop-floor visibility software to mid-size Indian manufacturers — companies doing ₹200 crore to ₹2,000 crore in annual revenue, mostly auto-component and engineering-goods firms in the industrial belts around Pune, Coimbatore, and the NCR. The company had closed a $12 million Series C four months earlier, and its lead investor, a partner who had previously sat on the board of two enterprise software companies that stalled at $10 million in annual recurring revenue, had asked for one thing ahead of this meeting: "Send me the strategy, not the roadmap." Ananya had sent the Jira export anyway, because until that week she had not been entirely sure what the difference was supposed to be, and neither, if she was honest, had anyone else in the room.

The stakes were not abstract. Parisar's ARR stood at ₹38 crore, growing at roughly 60 percent year over year, but churn in the mid-market segment had ticked up from 8 percent to 14 percent over two quarters, and three of the five customers who had left had given the same exit reason: "we could not tell where this product was going." The company's own engineering organisation — thirty-four people, up from nineteen a year earlier — was beginning to show the same symptom internally. Sprint plans were detailed and well-estimated. But when a new engineering manager asked, in her second week, "why is predictive maintenance scheduled after multi-tenant theming and not before it," nobody in the room could answer with anything sturdier than "that's what was in the doc." A company can survive a wrong sequencing decision. It struggles to survive not knowing whether the decision was reasoned or accidental, because the next ten decisions will make the same kind of mistake for the same kind of reason.

Ananya's problem, stated precisely, was this: she had a document called a strategy that was actually a plan, no roadmap connecting the two, and a board and an engineering org each quietly aware that something in the translation chain was missing without being able to name which link had broken. Getting the vocabulary right was not pedantry. It was the only way to find the broken link.

2. The idea, defined precisely

Strategy, roadmap, and plan are three different documents answering three different questions, at three different levels of certainty, on three different time horizons — and a great deal of organisational dysfunction traces back to treating any two of them as interchangeable.

Strategy is a coherent set of choices about where to compete and how to win there, given a specific diagnosis of the competitive situation and the constraints the company actually faces. The clearest modern formulation comes from the UCLA strategist Richard Rumelt, who in his 2011 book Good Strategy / Bad Strategy described a strategy's "kernel" as having three parts: a diagnosis of the situation that names what actually matters, a guiding policy for dealing with it, and a set of coherent actions that carry out the policy. Michael Porter's earlier work at Harvard, from the late 1970s onward, supplied the underlying logic — that strategy is fundamentally about choosing what not to do, because trying to be good at everything for everyone is not a strategy, it is an absence of one. A strategy, properly written, always contains a forgone alternative: a competitor you are choosing not to fight head-on, a segment you are choosing not to serve yet, a feature category you are choosing to leave to someone else.

Roadmap is the sequenced, directional translation of that strategy into themes and outcomes across a medium time horizon — typically two to four quarters — organised to show what will be tackled first, next, and later, and why that order follows from the strategic choices above it, rather than from whoever asked loudest in the last sales call. The product-management literature crystallised this distinction relatively recently: C. Todd Lombardo, Bruce McCarthy, Evan Ryan, and Michael Connors's Product Roadmaps Relaunched (2017) is generally credited with popularising the "outcome roadmap" — organised around themes and goals rather than a list of shipped features — as a corrective to roadmaps that were really just prioritised backlogs wearing a calendar. A roadmap should still be wrong sometimes, and should change when the evidence changes; its job is to show sequencing logic, not to promise dates.

Plan is the scheduled, resourced, owned commitment that turns a roadmap theme into work: which engineers, which sprints, which acceptance criteria, which date, who is accountable if it slips. A plan is the layer where dates are supposed to mean something, because a named person has committed named capacity against a named scope. All three descend from a company's vision and mission — the long-horizon statement of what future the company is trying to bring about — which sits above strategy and rarely changes at all.

Fig. 1 — Each layer down is more detailed, more certain in its dates, and expected to change more often. A slide that moves as fast as the plan but calls itself the strategy has confused two rows of this ladder.

3. How the translation actually works

The mechanics are best seen by walking the ladder in the order Parisar Analytics should have built it, rather than the order most teams accidentally build it — which is usually plan first, roadmap as an afterthought, and strategy as an annual slide nobody re-reads.

Step one is stating the vision in a sentence stable enough to survive several strategies. Parisar's was: "By 2030, every mid-size Indian manufacturer runs its shop floor with the same real-time visibility a Fortune 500 plant manager already has." Notice what this sentence does not do — it does not say how, or by when for any given customer, or which segment first. That looseness is deliberate; a vision that is too specific becomes a strategy by accident and stops being able to outlive one.

Step two is diagnosis, the first third of Rumelt's kernel, and the step most teams skip because it feels like stalling rather than working. Ananya's honest diagnosis, once she sat down to write it, was uncomfortable: enterprise players like SAP's manufacturing integration suite and Siemens's plant software were too expensive and too slow to deploy for a ₹300 crore auto-parts company, taking six to nine months and requiring a systems-integrator budget most such firms did not have; but local system integrators offered only point solutions — a dashboard here, a sensor kit there — with no platform underneath, so customers accumulated technical debt instead of a data asset. Parisar's own churn data supported the diagnosis: the customers who left were the ones for whom the six-week onboarding felt indistinguishable from the enterprise players' nine-month one, just cheaper.

Step three is the guiding policy — the sentence Ananya could say in a board meeting without sounding glib: "We win the mid-market by being the fastest platform to first value, and by being the system of record for machine data, not just the prettiest dashboard on top of someone else's." This single sentence does actual work. It rules things out. It means Parisar does not chase the largest enterprise accounts SAP already owns, does not compete purely on dashboard aesthetics, and prioritises the plumbing — sensor onboarding, data normalisation — over surface features, even when a customer is loudly asking for the latter.

Step four is coherent action, which is where roadmap begins: translating the guiding policy into two to four themes for the next several quarters, each theme stated as an outcome rather than a feature, each with an explicit "why now" that traces back to the guiding policy. "Reduce time-to-first-dashboard from six weeks to ten days" is a theme; "OCR nameplate scanning" is a feature that might serve that theme, and belongs one level down, in the plan.

Step five, the one practitioners most often leave implicit, is naming what the roadmap is not committing to. A roadmap that lists "Now / Next / Later" without also stating which currently-requested items were deliberately placed in Later, and why, invites every stakeholder to assume their pet item was simply forgotten rather than sequenced. Parisar's roadmap review deck began, from that October onward, with a slide titled "What we are choosing not to do this half" — a discipline borrowed directly from Rumelt's insistence that a strategy names its forgone alternatives, applied one layer down.

Step six is the handoff to plan: each roadmap theme, once a quarter starts, gets broken into scoped, estimated, owned sprints with real dates — the layer where "10 days" becomes "sprint 14, ending 24 November 2025, owned by Rohan Iyer."

4. A worked example, with the arithmetic shown

Parisar's "Now" theme — cut onboarding from six weeks to ten days — needed to become a Q3 FY26 (October–December 2025) delivery plan. The engineering org assigned fourteen engineers to it, working in two-week sprints, with a trailing-twelve-sprint average velocity of eight story points per engineer per sprint. A quarter holds six two-week sprints. That gives a raw capacity of 14 × 8 × 6 = 672 story points for the quarter.

Two features were scoped against that budget: an OCR-based nameplate scanner that reads a machine's model and serial number from a photograph instead of a manual data-entry form, estimated at 240 points; and an auto PLC (programmable logic controller) tag-mapping engine that infers which sensor signal corresponds to which machine parameter, estimated at 400 points. Together, 640 points — 95 percent of the quarter's 672-point budget, leaving a 32-point, roughly 5 percent buffer. Ananya flagged this in the planning review as thin rather than healthy; a plan run at 95 percent of nominal capacity has almost no room to absorb the ordinary friction of a real quarter — a production incident, a departing engineer, a customer escalation.

Four weeks into the quarter, a top-five customer, Prithvi Forge Works, a Faridabad-based forging company, reported a production-blocking data-mismatch bug, and Parisar pulled four engineers off the theme for two full sprints to resolve it and stabilise the customer relationship.
