This is where the three documents earned their keep by behaving differently on purpose. The plan absorbed the shock directly: the PLC auto-mapping feature was rescoped from covering twelve PLC brands to the five brands that covered 90 percent of Parisar's installed base, trimming it from 400 points to roughly 340, which brought total scope to 580 points against 608 points of revised capacity — a plan that was replanned, visibly, with a name (Suresh Bhatt, the engineering lead) attached to the rescoping decision. The roadmap theme itself — "cut onboarding to ten days" — did not need to change at all, because the rescoped plan still delivered the outcome for the segment that mattered, and the roadmap review that quarter simply noted the narrower PLC coverage as a known limitation to revisit in the "Next" theme. The strategy — win via speed-to-value and ownership of the machine-data layer — was never in question, because nothing about a four-week firefight at one customer changed the underlying diagnosis of the market. A shock that reaches all three layers simultaneously is usually a sign that the layers were never properly separated to begin with.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

A roadmap is a bet map, not a prioritised backlog with a calendar bolted on

The single most common corruption of a roadmap is a list of features ranked by whoever shouted last, with quarters attached to make it look planned. A genuine roadmap item carries a "why now" that traces to the guiding policy above it; if you cannot state that sentence for an item, it is a wish, not a roadmap entry, however confidently it sits in a Q2 column.

Certainty should decrease as you go up the ladder, and detail should decrease with it

Strategy should be the most stable and least detailed layer; the plan should be the most volatile and most detailed. When people get angry that "the roadmap slipped," the anger is often a category error — only the plan was ever supposed to carry date accountability. The roadmap tells you sequencing logic, not a delivery promise.

"No roadmap" and "no strategy" are two different diseases

A company can have a sharp strategy and jump straight to sprint plans with nothing translating between them — engineers guessing at sequencing from Slack messages. Or it can run an elaborate, well-groomed roadmap sitting on nothing: a compilation of competitor features, sales promises, and conference-talk ideas with no guiding policy underneath. Both look productive from a distance. Neither is.

OKRs are not a fourth layer; they are the measurement bridge

Objectives and Key Results, the goal-setting method Intel's Andy Grove developed and John Doerr later popularised at Google, sit between strategy and roadmap as an accountability mechanism, not as a fifth document to maintain. The Objective restates a strategic aspiration in energising language; the Key Results are the numbers that tell you whether a given roadmap theme is actually working. Teams that treat OKRs as a parallel planning ritual, disconnected from both the strategy above and the roadmap below, end up with three uncoordinated documents instead of two coordinated ones.

The document's title on the slide is not evidence of what it actually is

Ananya's "Product Strategy FY26" slide was, functionally, a plan — dated features with owners and no stated alternative forgone. Diagnose a document by asking three questions regardless of its title: does it name a choice with a real alternative given up? Does it specify sequencing logic rather than just an order? Does it commit named capacity to named dates? A document can answer only the first and still deserve the word strategy; a document that only answers the third is a plan no matter what its header says.

Strategy exists at more than one altitude, and confusing altitudes causes real arguments

Corporate strategy, business-unit strategy, and product-line strategy nest inside one another. "Expand into predictive maintenance" can legitimately be strategy at the product-line altitude — a genuine choice about where that product competes — while simultaneously being merely a roadmap theme relative to Parisar's corporate strategy of owning the machine-data layer. Arguments about whether something "belongs on the roadmap or the strategy" are sometimes really disagreements about which altitude is being discussed.

None of the three layers tells you whether the underlying diagnosis is correct

A crisply written Rumelt kernel, a well-sequenced roadmap, and a tightly resourced plan can all be internally coherent and still be wrong about the market — if the diagnosis that churn was caused by slow onboarding was itself mistaken, everything built on it inherits the error faithfully. The framework forces assumptions into the open where they can be tested; it does not test them for you.

Some organisations legitimately skip a layer, and that is not always a failure

A two-person, pre-seed company may have almost no gap between strategy and plan, because the time horizons are already close together — next month's plan and next year's strategy can be the same six-week bet. Skipping the roadmap document is fine there, provided the founders can still answer "why this next, and why not something else" without the answer collapsing into "we felt like it."

6. How this looks different by product type and by company stage

In consumer products, strategy is usually a statement about which growth loop or network effect the company is trying to compound — a food-delivery app choosing to win on delivery speed rather than restaurant selection, say — and the roadmap is organised around experiment velocity rather than large themes, because the unit of progress is often a weekly or fortnightly A/B test rather than a quarter-long build. The plan, correspondingly, is measured in experiment slots and traffic allocation rather than story points.

In B2B products like Parisar's, strategy centres on the ideal customer profile and the land-and-expand motion — which segment to win first and how the product widens within an account afterward — and the roadmap is disproportionately shaped by named-account commitments and renewal risk, since a single enterprise logo's renewal date can reasonably move a roadmap theme forward. The plan is tied tightly to the customer-success and sales calendar: quarterly business reviews, renewal dates, and contractual delivery commitments carry weight a consumer roadmap rarely has to accommodate.

In marketplace products, strategy is a choice about which side of the market to subsidise and what liquidity threshold — the minimum density of supply and demand in a given city or category — makes the marketplace self-sustaining without further subsidy. The roadmap is often organised geographically or by category, sequenced by which markets are closest to that liquidity threshold, and the plan resembles a city-launch calendar as much as a feature calendar.

Company stage changes the weight, not the logic. An early-stage company often holds strategy in the founders' heads and a single shared document doubling as both roadmap and plan, which is defensible as long as the "why this, why not that" reasoning survives being said out loud. A large company — Parisar at, say, five hundred employees and multiple product lines — needs strategy owned explicitly at the executive level, a roadmap that a programme-management function reconciles across product lines for shared dependencies, and a plan layer formal enough to carry RAID logs (risks, assumptions, issues, dependencies) and feed an annual operating plan the finance function can budget against. The translation ladder does not change; the formality of each rung does.

7. Common mistakes, and how to catch them cheaply

The roadmap slips every quarter and nobody treats it as news. The underlying misunderstanding is planning-as-roadmapping: dates were implied without a resourced, owned plan standing behind them. The cheap diagnostic: ask "if this theme moved from Q3 to Q1 next year, what actually changes?" If the honest answer is "nothing, we simply have not gotten to it," the item was a plan wearing a roadmap's clothes, with none of a plan's accountability infrastructure.

The annual strategy off-site produces a handsome deck that nobody downstream can connect to their actual work. The misunderstanding is treating strategy as an annual ritual rather than a living input with a translation mechanism feeding it into the roadmap continuously. The cheap diagnostic: pick any three items on this quarter's roadmap and ask an engineer, unprompted, which sentence of the strategy deck each one serves. Silence is the finding.

The plan is airtight, on schedule, beautifully Gantt-charted — and delivers something the market stopped wanting two quarters ago. The misunderstanding is mistaking planning precision for strategic correctness, because a plan feels controllable in a way strategy rarely does, so teams over-invest in the layer that rewards effort with visible progress. The cheap diagnostic: ask when the strategic diagnosis underneath this plan was last checked against new data. If the answer predates the plan's own kickoff, the plan may be flawlessly executing something already stale.

Two different roadmap documents exist for the same product, each cited by a different stakeholder to support what they already wanted to believe. The misunderstanding is not about content but about ownership: no one function was ever assigned the job of translating strategy into roadmap, so sales, engineering, and product each drafted their own. The cheap diagnostic: ask "if strategy changed tomorrow, whose job is it to update the roadmap, and how would the plan owners find out?" A blank stare locates the defect precisely.

8. What good looks like

Six weeks after that board meeting, Ananya's team had rebuilt the ladder rather than patched the slide. The strategy — one paragraph, Rumelt-shaped, reviewed twice a year — lived on a single page that had not changed since the rewrite. The roadmap sat one level below it: three themes per half, each with an explicit "why now" sentence linking back to a phrase in the strategy paragraph, and an explicit "not now" list naming what had been deliberately deferred, reviewed and allowed to change every quarter. Beneath that sat the plan — Jira, sprint-scoped, owned by named engineering leads, with dates that were genuine commitments precisely because nothing above them pretended to be a date. Two Key Results — time-to-first-dashboard, and quarterly churn in the mid-market segment — sat as hyperlinked scorecards between the strategy and the roadmap, so that anyone could trace, in under a minute, from a single sprint ticket up to the sentence about winning on speed and data ownership that justified its existence. When the board partner who had asked for "the strategy, not the roadmap" saw the one-page document in December, his only question was whether Parisar could hold the paragraph unchanged for two years. Ananya said yes, and for once she was confident that was the right answer to be confident about.

9. What Ananya decided, and what to read next

Ananya's decision was not to write a new strategy — the guiding policy about speed and data ownership held up under scrutiny — but to stop letting the Jira export impersonate it, and to build the missing middle rung explicitly, with OKRs as its handrail. The Q3 capacity shock at Prithvi Forge Works had shown the ladder working as designed: the plan absorbed the hit, the roadmap theme survived unchanged, and the strategy was never in question, because the three layers had finally been separated enough to fail independently instead of together.

The natural next topic is OKRs themselves — how an Objective is chosen so it is neither a restated strategy sentence nor a disguised feature list, and how Key Results are chosen so they measure an outcome rather than an activity, since the bridge between strategy and roadmap is exactly where most quarterly planning cycles quietly break down. After that, portfolio roadmapping — reconciling several product lines' roadmaps against shared engineering capacity and shared strategic bets — becomes necessary the moment a company like Parisar has more than one product line pulling on the same thirty-four engineers.

Two questions worth sitting with:

1. Pick a document at your own workplace that someone calls a "strategy." Does it name a real alternative that was given up — and if you removed the pages of features and dates, would anything be left?

2. When your roadmap last "slipped," was it the roadmap that moved, or was it actually the plan underneath it — and did anyone in the room know the difference at the time?

Manzar Fulfilment Cloud: One Deck, Three Audiences

Telling strategy, roadmap and plan apart — and knowing which one a document has to be

1. The scene

On the evening of Monday, 21 September 2026, Arjun Mehta sat in Manzar Fulfilment Cloud's office off Bengaluru's Sarjapur Road with one slide deck open and two people waiting on it. As Vice President of Product, Arjun had until Thursday evening to send the board its pre-read for Friday's meeting, where the FY27 plan would be presented and, he suspected, questioned line by line. He also had until Wednesday noon to send an externally shareable version of the same material to Rohan Fernandes, Manzar's sales head, who needed it to close a renewal in Dubai before the client's quarter-end budget review on 30 September. Arjun had one draft, called the "FY27 Product Plan," that tried to be the board's strategy, the company's roadmap and the client's delivery commitment at once — and he suspected that mixture had already cost the company money once this year.

2. Company background

Manzar Fulfilment Cloud was founded in 2019 by Neha Kulkarni, a former operations manager at a large e-commerce logistics arm, to sell warehouse-and-order-management software to Indian D2C brands and quick-commerce dark-store operators — the layer that decides which warehouse picks an order, in what sequence, and how inventory reconciles across channels. By September 2026 it served about 145 clients, carried roughly ₹38 crore in annual recurring revenue, and had raised ₹95 crore in a Series B from a Bengaluru-based growth fund fourteen months earlier. Its engineering team split across Bengaluru and Pune; its closest rivals for the same mid-market accounts were Increff and Unicommerce, with Shiprocket and ClickPost competing at the smaller end. Eight months earlier, Manzar had opened its first account outside India: Marjan Retail Group, a fast-growing Dubai grocery-and-general-merchandise chain opening dark stores to compete with instant-delivery apps across the UAE. Marjan's current contract was worth ₹4.2 crore a year, and its procurement team was now deciding whether to sign a ₹6.5 crore expansion covering two more emirates.

3. The situation

The trouble had a precedent, laid out in Exhibit 3. In the June quarter, Manzar had sent one of its large fashion D2C accounts in Mumbai a deck labelled "roadmap," listing a multi-warehouse slotting AI feature against a printed quarter and week. The client's operations head read the printed date as a commitment. When the feature slipped ten weeks past that date, the client escalated to Neha directly, and Manzar issued an ₹18 lakh service credit and watched the account's renewal terms move from annual to quarterly notice (Exhibit 2). Wei Ling Tan, Manzar's customer success lead in Singapore, had run that relationship end to end and did not want to run it again at four times the contract value.

That was exactly the shape of what was in front of Arjun now. Rohan Fernandes, working the Marjan renewal from New Jersey, had told the client's procurement team that the same multi-warehouse slotting AI, plus an Arabic-language pick-list module, would ship on a schedule he could put in the contract addendum. Lukas Berger, Manzar's lead product designer in Berlin, was adamant that the slotting AI was not ready to be named on any dated document: Daniel Cho, a data scientist in Toronto, had just reported pilot accuracy still climbing at both test warehouses (Exhibit 2), with a third pilot not scheduled until December and no guarantee the model would generalise to Marjan's Dubai layout. Neha, for her part, wanted the board to see three multi-year bets — owning fulfilment software for dark-store retail, becoming the default OS for cross-border D2C logistics, and building an AI layer on top of both — and was wary of a dated feature grid inviting the scrutiny that had unsettled the June board meeting.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Option A — One deck, with a caveat

Keep the single "FY27 Product Plan" deck, add a line noting that dates beyond the current quarter are indicative, and send the same file to the board and to Marjan. This costs Arjun no extra time before Thursday. Its weakness is the one June already exposed: procurement teams read date grids, not footnotes, and Rohan still needs a signable commitment that a caveat does not provide.

Option B — Split into three artifacts

Produce three separate documents: a one-page strategy note naming Manzar's multi-year bets for the board; an 18-month roadmap of quarterly themes, with the slotting AI and Arabic pick-list shown as themes under evaluation rather than dated items; and a locked Q1 FY27 delivery plan, resourced and dated, that becomes the contractual basis for Marjan's addendum for only what the team can commit to this quarter. OKRs tie the roadmap's themes to the plan's quarterly commitments, so the three read as one story, not three unrelated papers. This takes more work before Thursday and requires Neha and Rohan to tell Marjan that some features are not yet datable — harder than Option A, but consistent with what June already proved.

Option C — Two tracks, unreconciled

Let Rohan issue Marjan a separate, more optimistic commercial roadmap with dates running through Q3, while Product keeps its own looser internal roadmap unchanged. This closes the deal fastest and keeps engineering's planning flexible. It also recreates June's failure mode in a starker form: two documents describing the same features differently, discoverable by anyone on Marjan's side who compares notes, at four times the contract value.

8. A note for the learner

The lens this case asks you to apply is simple to state and easy to skip under deadline pressure: before a document leaves the building, know whether it is a strategy, a roadmap or a plan, because each promises something different to the person reading it. A strategy promises a direction that will not move with each sprint. A roadmap promises a sequence of themes that will be revisited every quarter as evidence changes. A plan promises specific work, by specific people, by a specific date — the only one of the three that belongs in a contract. Manzar's June failure was not a forecasting error; it was a category error, a roadmap dressed as a plan and read that way by a client with money at stake.

A well-reasoned answer treats Option B as the defensible path, not because it is the easiest, but because it puts each promise in front of the audience that can be held to it. The board gets a strategy note that will not need revising when a pilot slips. Marjan gets a plan for the quarter that engineering has actually resourced, a stronger commercial signal than a longer list of undated hopes. The roadmap keeps the slotting AI honestly labelled as a theme under test, protecting Lukas's team from being blamed for a technology that still needs its December pilot. The harder conversation — telling Rohan, and through him Marjan, that two features are themes, not commitments, until the plan says otherwise — is the conversation June's credit note already paid for in advance.
